business_model.claim: Volaris is an ultra-low-cost carrier (ULCC) that sells air passenger transportation on point-to-point routes connecting 44 cities in Mexico, 22 cities in the United States, four cities in Central America and two cities in South America, operating up to 550 average daily flight segments on a 155-aircraft Airbus A320 family fleet.
quotes: We are a ULCC incorporated under the laws of Mexico.

we have increased our routes from five to more than 220 and grown our cost-efficient Airbus A320 family aircraft from four to 155 as of December 31, 2025. We currently operate up to 550 average daily flight segments on routes that connect 44 cities in Mexico, 22 cities in the United States, four cities in Central America and two cities in South America.

business_model.basis: stated in F2 (20-F income statement) and P3 (20-F Item 5)
business_model.claim: In 2025, 43% of total operating revenues came from passenger fare revenues of $1,301,750 (table in thousands), 52% from other passenger revenues of $1,580,665 (table in thousands), and 5% from non-passenger revenues (other non-passenger revenues of $134,483 plus cargo of $20,618, both in thousands).
quotes: 43% of our total operating revenues were derived from passenger fares in 2025.
52% of our total operating revenues were derived from other passenger revenues in 2025.
In 2025, we derived U.S.$155.1 million, or 5%, of our total operating revenues from these sources.

business_model.basis: stated in P1 (20-F Item 4) and P3 (20-F Item 5)
business_model.claim: Volaris targets VFR (visiting friends and relatives) travelers, leisure travelers, and cost-conscious business travelers, with an average base fare of U.S. $42.0 in 2025 and promotional fares as low as U.S. $0.05 (MXN $1), pricing base fares to compete with long-distance bus fares in Mexico.
quotes: Our main competitive advantages are our low base fares and our focus on VFR travelers, leisure travelers and cost-conscious business travelers.
During 2025, our average base fare was U.S. $42.0, and we regularly offered promotional fares as low as U.S. $0.05 (MXN $1), excluding airport fees.

business_model.basis: stated in P3 (20-F Item 5) and P1 (20-F Item 4)
business_model.claim: Revenue is driven by capacity (available seat miles), load factor, and average passenger revenue per booked passenger; in 2025 the average load factor was 84.3%.
quotes: Passenger revenues are based upon our capacity, load factor and the average passenger revenue per booked passenger.

In 2025, our average load factor was 84.3%, compared to an average load factor of 85.2 % for the other Latin American publicly traded airlines and 82.1% for our U.S.-based publicly traded target market competitors.

business_model.basis: stated in F2 (20-F income statement) and P3 (20-F Item 5)
business_model.claim: Fuel is the single largest operating expense, at $885,520 (table in thousands) in 2025, representing 31% of total operating costs; other major cost lines include landing/take-off/navigation expenses ($544,298), salaries and benefits ($451,096), and depreciation of right-of-use assets ($448,570), all in thousands.
quotes: Fuel expense is our single largest operating expense.

Fuel is our largest cost, representing 31% of our total operating expense in 2025, and continuous volatility in fuel costs or significant disruptions in the supply of fuel could have a material adverse effect on our business, statements of operations and financial position.

business_model.basis: stated in P1 (20-F Item 4) and P3 (20-F Item 5)
business_model.claim: Volaris's CASM in 2025 was U.S. 8.04 cents, compared to an average of U.S. 11.12 cents for other Latin American publicly traded airlines and U.S. 16.77 cents for its U.S.-based publicly traded target market competitors, which the company attributes to its efficient uniform fleet, high asset utilization, direct sales focus, and variable performance-based compensation.
quotes: In 2025, our CASM was U.S. 8.04 cents, compared to an average non-stage-length adjusted CASM of U.S. 11.12 cents for the other Latin American publicly traded airlines, including Aeroméxico, Copa, and LATAM.

We also have lower costs than our U.S.-based publicly traded target market competitors, including Alaska, Allegiant, American, Delta, Frontier, JetBlue, Southwest, and United, which had an average non-stage-length adjusted CASM of U.S. 16.77 cents in 2025.

growth_thesis.claim: Fleet and route expansion: Volaris grew its Airbus A320 family fleet from four to 155 aircraft and operates up to 550 average daily flight segments across 44 Mexican, 22 U.S., 4 Central American, and 2 South American cities; for this to continue it must keep acquiring or leasing A320neo-family aircraft and identify new profitable routes.

We currently operate up to 550 average daily flight segments on routes that connect 44 cities in Mexico, 22 cities in the United States, four cities in Central America and two cities in South America.

growth_thesis.basis: Stated in P1 with peer comparisons; the specific drivers are company-stated, not independently verified.
growth_thesis.claim: Structural unit-cost advantage: Volaris's 2025 CASM of U.S. 8.04 cents was well below the 11.12-cent Latin American peer average and the 16.77-cent U.S. peer average; for this gap to persist it must maintain a uniform A320-family fleet, high asset utilization, direct-sales emphasis, and a variable performance-based compensation structure.
quotes: In 2025, our CASM was U.S. 8.04 cents, compared to an average non-stage-length adjusted CASM of U.S. 11.12 cents for the other Latin American publicly traded airlines, including Aeroméxico, Copa, and LATAM.

We also have lower costs than our U.S.-based publicly traded target market competitors, including Alaska, Allegiant, American, Delta, Frontier, JetBlue, Southwest, and United, which had an average non-stage-length adjusted CASM of U.S. 16.77 cents in 2025.

growth_thesis.basis: Stated in P3 (52% figure, unbundling description) and F2 (dollar amounts); the growth linkage is inferred from the three-year revenue trend in F2.
growth_thesis.claim: Ancillary (non-fare) revenue growth through unbundling: Other passenger revenues reached $1,580,665 (table in thousands) in 2025, representing 52% of total operating revenues; for this to continue it must sustain high load factors so that a large passenger base purchases baggage, seat selection, and other paid services.
quotes: 52% of our total operating revenues were derived from other passenger revenues in 2025.
This unbundling strategy has allowed us to significantly grow our non-passenger revenue and total revenue.

growth_thesis.basis: Stated in P1 (fare, load factor figures); the bus-to-air conversion claim is a company strategy description, not quantified in the evidence.
growth_thesis.claim: Ultra-low base fares stimulating demand and converting bus travelers: Volaris's 2025 average base fare was U.S. $42.0 with promotional fares as low as MXN $1, and an average load factor of 84.3%; for this to continue it must maintain a cost structure low enough to sustain sub-$50 fares while covering all operating costs.
quotes: During 2025, our average base fare was U.S. $42.0, and we regularly offered promotional fares as low as U.S. $0.05 (MXN $1), excluding airport fees.

In 2025, our average load factor was 84.3%, compared to an average load factor of 85.2 % for the other Latin American publicly traded airlines and 82.1% for our U.S.-based publicly traded target market competitors.

growth_thesis.basis: Stated in P1 and P3 (ownership split, regulatory conditions, market share figures); the scale-economy benefit is inferred from the company's stated strategy, not quantified.

quotes: the pre-Merger shareholders of Viva and Volaris will hold approximately 48% and 50% of the Combined Company's capital stock, respectively

In 2025, the two Mexican ultra low-cost carriers, Volaris and Aeroenlaces Nacionales, held 73.5% of the domestic market based on passenger flight segments. Volaris had 34.0% of the domestic market, according to the AFAC.

growth_thesis.basis: Stated in P1 (subsidiary dates, expansion intent); the profitability condition is inferred from the ULCC model's requirement for sufficient volume.
growth_thesis.claim: International expansion in Central and South America: Volaris operates subsidiaries in Costa Rica (since December 2016) and El Salvador (since September 2021) and states it seeks to replicate its ULCC model in the region; for this to continue it must find sufficient demand in each new market to make the low-fare, point-to-point model profitable.
quotes: our operating subsidiary in Costa Rica, Vuela Aviación, began operations on December 1, 2016, and our operating subsidiary in El Salvador, Vuela El Salvador, began operations on September 15, 2021. We seek to replicate our ultra-low-cost model in Central and South America by offering low base fares and point-to-point service in the region.

growth_thesis.basis: Stated in P1 (agreement names, purpose); the revenue impact is not quantified in any cited item.
growth_thesis.claim: Codeshare network expansion: In 2025 Volaris entered codeshare agreements with Copa Airlines, Iberia, and Hainan Airlines in addition to its existing Frontier arrangement; for this to drive growth it must maintain these partnerships and the partner airlines must continue serving overlapping destinations.
quotes: In 2025, we entered into additional codeshare agreements with Copa Airlines, Iberia and Hainan Airlines as part of our efforts to expand our network connectivity, complementing our existing arrangement with Frontier Airlines.
